title: Justification, reporting & storing images
blurb: The paper trail behind every radiograph: checking previous images, recording justification, clinical evaluation, and storing and sharing images securely.
question: A new patient tells the dentist she had bitewings at her old practice three months ago, and asks why she needs 'more X-rays' at all. After the examination, the dentist decides one periapical is needed. What should happen before, during and after that exposure so the records are complete and lawful?

teach.h: Every radiograph leaves a paper trail
teach.body: A radiograph is only lawful if it is justified, and only useful if someone looks at it properly and records what they find. IR(ME)R 2017 and good record-keeping therefore expect a clear trail for every exposure: why it was taken and who authorised it, who took it and how, what it showed, and where it is now stored. As the dental nurse you often prepare, check and file these records, so you are a key part of keeping that trail complete.

teach.caption: There is no justification for routine radiographs of new patients without a clinical examination. Previous images, including from other practices, must be taken into account.

teach.h: Justification and talking to the patient
teach.body: The IR(ME)R practitioner, usually the dentist, justifies each exposure and records it as an authorisation, for example a signature or secure electronic initials. If a patient asks why an X-ray is needed, explain that the dentist has judged it necessary to diagnose or plan treatment, and that the dose is small, comparable to a few days of natural background radiation. If a patient says she may be pregnant, follow the local pregnancy enquiry procedure and tell the dentist, who reviews the justification.

teach.body: Every exposure must have a clinical evaluation, recorded by a trained person (usually the dentist). It covers the whole image, including areas outside the tooth of interest, and should be done the same day where possible. It needn't be a long report: charting caries, noting findings that affect treatment, or 'root form simple' before an extraction are all acceptable. If no evaluation is recorded, the exposure can't be shown to have been justified. Dental nurses don't diagnose, but you can make sure the entry is there.

items.label: Check previous images; justify and authorise
Identify, position, expose; grade A or N
Included in the image quality audit

teach.body: Radiographs are part of the patient's dental record and are confidential personal health data under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. Label every image with the right patient, date and orientation; an image filed against the wrong patient may mean a repeat exposure. Keep digital images on secure, password-protected, backed-up systems, and keep films mounted and stored safely. Share them only securely and for a proper purpose, such as a referral, keeping the original. Patients have a right to access their records.

children's records generally, or 26th if 17 when treatment ended

teach.caption: From the NHS Records Management Code of Practice retention schedule. Follow your practice's local retention policy for children's records.

teach.text: Image quality grading (A/N) is NOT the same as clinical evaluation. Grading asks 'is the picture technically good enough?'; evaluation asks 'what does it show?' Both must be recorded.

items: Check and obtain previous radiographs, including from other practices, to avoid unnecessary repeats.
The dentist justifies and authorises every exposure; tell the dentist about any possible pregnancy.
Record identity, authorisation, view, operator, settings and repeats, A/N grade and clinical evaluation.
Images are confidential records: label correctly, store securely, keep for 11 years (children to age 25 or 26).

summary: You can now explain why previous radiographs are checked, how justification and authorisation are recorded, what to tell a patient who asks why an X-ray is needed, what the record of each exposure must contain, what a clinical evaluation is, and how images are stored, shared and retained.

A.q: A new patient says she had radiographs at another practice recently. Why should these be requested before taking new ones?
options: To check the old practice's fees
To avoid an unnecessary repeat exposure
Because new images can't be taken for a year
To copy the other practice's diagnosis
A.why: Previous radiographs must be taken into account when justifying; recent diagnostic images may make a new exposure unnecessary.

whyNot.0: Fees have nothing to do with radiation protection.
whyNot.2: There's no fixed waiting period; each exposure is judged on its own justification.
whyNot.3: The dentist makes their own diagnosis; previous images inform it.

A.q: A patient asks why she needs a radiograph today. What is the most appropriate response?
options: 'It's practice policy for everyone.'
'It's free, so you might as well.'
'We have to use the X-ray machine regularly.'
'The dentist needs it to diagnose properly.'
A.why: Every exposure must be justified: the dentist has decided it's needed for diagnosis or treatment planning.

whyNot.0: Routine radiographs for everyone aren't justified under IR(ME)R.
whyNot.1: Cost is never a reason for exposing a patient.
whyNot.2: Equipment use is not a justification for exposure.

A.q: What must be recorded for every radiograph after it has been taken?
options: A clinical evaluation of the image
The patient's next routine recall date
The operator's home address
A copy of the local rules
A.why: IR(ME)R requires a clinical evaluation of each exposure to be carried out and recorded.

whyNot.1: Recall dates are part of general care, not the radiograph record.
whyNot.2: Staff home addresses aren't part of patient records.
whyNot.3: Local rules are a practice document, not part of each patient's record.

B.q: How long should adult dental records, including radiographs, be kept under the current NHS retention schedule?
options: 2 years
5 years
15 years
11 years
B.why: Dental records are kept for 11 years; this changed from 15 years in May 2023.

whyNot.0: 2 years applies to some finance records, not clinical records.
whyNot.1: 5 years is too short for clinical records.
whyNot.2: 15 years was the old period, replaced in May 2023.

B.q: A patient says she might be pregnant just before her radiograph. What should the dental nurse do?
options: Proceed, as dental doses are very low
Follow procedure; tell the dentist
Fit a lead apron and continue
Cancel all her future radiographs
B.why: Follow the practice's pregnancy enquiry procedure and inform the dentist, who reviews whether the exposure is still justified.

whyNot.0: The nurse can't decide to proceed; the dentist must review the justification.
whyNot.2: Lead aprons are not routinely justified, and an apron doesn't replace the procedure.
whyNot.3: Future radiographs are judged individually; blanket cancellation isn't appropriate.

B.q: Which statement about clinical evaluation is correct?
options: It only covers the tooth requested
It is the same as A/N grading
It should cover the whole image
The dental nurse writes the diagnosis
B.why: The clinical evaluation must cover the whole image, including areas outside the region of interest.

whyNot.0: Findings outside the area of interest must be considered too.
whyNot.1: A/N grading rates technical quality; evaluation interprets the image.
whyNot.3: Dental nurses don't diagnose; evaluation is done by a trained operator, usually the dentist.

C.q: Under which law are radiographs protected as confidential personal data?
options: COSHH Regulations 2002
The RIDDOR Regulations 2013
UK GDPR and the DPA 2018
IRR17 on its own
C.why: Radiographs are health data in the patient record, protected under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act (DPA) 2018.

whyNot.1: RIDDOR covers reporting injuries and dangerous occurrences.
whyNot.3: IRR17 covers radiation protection of staff and public, not data confidentiality.

C.q: A periapical is accidentally saved to the wrong patient's record. What is the main risk?
options: The image will be over-exposed
The receptor will be damaged
The practice fails its QA target
A repeat exposure may be needed
C.why: If the image can't be found under the right patient, it may have to be retaken, adding unnecessary dose; it is also a confidentiality breach.

whyNot.0: Filing doesn't change the exposure of the image.
whyNot.1: Saving a file can't damage the receptor.
whyNot.2: QA targets relate to image quality grading, not filing errors.

C.q: How is the dentist's decision that an exposure is justified usually recorded?
options: As an authorisation in the notes
On the local rules
In the reject log
On a label on the X-ray unit itself
C.why: The justification decision is recorded as an authorisation, such as a signature or secure electronic initials in the clinical record.

whyNot.1: Local rules are IRR17 working instructions, not patient records.
whyNot.2: The reject log records faulty images.
whyNot.3: Nothing patient-specific is recorded on the X-ray unit.

reteach.title: A parcel with a tracking number
reteach.question: When you send an important parcel, why is it tracked at every step, and how is a radiograph like that?

blocks.body: A tracked parcel has a record of who ordered it, who packed it, when it was sent, that it arrived and was opened, and where it is now. A radiograph is the same. The dentist 'orders' it (justification and authorisation), the operator 'packs and sends' it (identity check, exposure, settings), the dentist 'opens' it (clinical evaluation), and it is then 'archived' securely for 11 years. A missing step, such as no evaluation, means you can't prove it was needed at all.

steps.sub: Justified and authorised by the dentist

blocks.text: If there's no clinical evaluation in the notes, the exposure can't be shown to have been justified.

explain.body: Before any new exposure, the dentist takes previous radiographs into account, including those from other practices. Recent, diagnostic images may make a repeat unnecessary.

test.q: Which factor must the IR(ME)R practitioner consider when justifying an exposure?
options: Any previous radiographs
The patient's insurance status
How busy the clinic is
The age of the X-ray unit
test.why: Justification must weigh the availability and findings of previous radiographs, along with the clinical need and the patient's age.

whyNot.1: Insurance has no role in justification.
whyNot.2: Workload is irrelevant to whether an exposure is needed.
whyNot.3: Equipment age is a QA matter, not a justification factor.

explain.body: The dentist justifies the exposure and records it as an authorisation, for example a signature or secure electronic initials. The reasoning doesn't have to be written down, but if an exposure is refused, the reason is recorded.

options: The patient's signed consent form
A record of the justification decision
The RPA's approval of the X-ray room
The HSE registration certificate
test.why: Authorisation is the documented record that the IR(ME)R practitioner has justified the exposure.

whyNot.2: RPA advice relates to IRR17 room design.
whyNot.3: HSE registration is an employer requirement under IRR17.

explain.body: Each image must be clinically evaluated and recorded by a trained person, usually the dentist, covering the whole image, ideally the same day. Short entries are fine, such as caries charting or 'root form simple'.

test.q: Which would be an acceptable clinical evaluation entry before an extraction?
options: 'Image taken.'
'Grade A.'
'Root form simple.'
'Exposure 0.1 s.'
test.why: Guidance gives 'root form simple' or 'hooked roots' as acceptable brief evaluations before an extraction.

whyNot.0: Stating an image was taken records nothing about what it shows.
whyNot.1: A grade is the quality rating, not an evaluation.
whyNot.3: Exposure settings describe how it was taken, not what it shows.

explain.body: Images are confidential records under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. Label them correctly, store them securely and back them up, share only securely and for a proper purpose, and keep them for 11 years (children generally to age 25, or 26 if 17 when treatment ended).

test.q: A specialist asks for a copy of a patient's radiograph for a referral. What is the best approach?
options: Post the original film with no record
Email it to any address given by phone
Refuse; images can never be shared
Send it securely and keep the original
test.why: Images may be shared for a proper purpose such as referral, using a secure method, with the original kept in the record.

whyNot.0: Sending the original loses it from the record.
whyNot.1: Unverified addresses risk a data breach.
whyNot.2: Sharing for referral is appropriate when done securely.
